toc.title: The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality
The next step: build your safety state
Benefit one: getting unstuck from a traumatized state
Benefit two: more distress tolerance for the basics of life
Benefit three: more distress tolerance for new challenges

blocks.p: You've learned the Polyvagal Theory, so now what? What do you do with this information?

I'm assuming you already have a decent understanding of it, and you're ready for what to do next. So I'm not going to spend any time here on the basics. What I want is to make sure you have a top-down understanding of what to do with the polyvagal information you've probably already gotten. Maybe you haven't been able to apply it as a bottom-up process quite yet, and that's okay.

blocks.h: The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality

blocks.p: The Polyvagal Theory is not a modality. It's not a set of techniques. It's not a therapy style. I think a lot of people confuse it with that. It's science. It's nerdy, it's academic, it's dense. It can be very overwhelming, and it can leave you wondering what the heck to do with that information.

Something I really recommend is that you keep going back and relearning aspects of the Polyvagal Theory. I do it every now and then, and I learn it in a different way, especially if I go back to one of the original writings from Dr. Porges, the creator of the Polyvagal Theory. Maybe read a more specific article on how it's applied. Get yourself to think about things a little differently. Get a new wrinkle in your brain about the Polyvagal Theory.

blocks.h: The next step: build your safety state

blocks.p: So let's say you've done all that. Now what?

The next step, in my opinion, is to build the strength of your safety state. I think this is always a good idea, whether you're stuck in a defensive state or not. It can be a good idea even if you're not working on relieving your trauma, and maybe you're just working on your own self-development.

Developing the strength of your safety state is actionable. There's a lot you can do about it. Maybe you've learned the Polyvagal Theory, but you're not really ready to start relieving your stuck defensive state, your trauma. You're not there yet, but you want to do something with what you've learned. Building your safety state is something you can do.
There are a whole bunch of potential benefits to developing the strength of your safety state. Here are three of them.

blocks.h: Benefit one: getting unstuck from a traumatized state

blocks.p: This might be the most obvious benefit. With a stronger vagal brake, a stronger safety state, comes greater distress tolerance. And with greater distress tolerance, there's probably going to be more interest and more motivation, or at least more space for them. There's more capacity to feel your stuck defensive state, and to allow some self-regulating [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing to happen.

Without a strong enough safety state, working on your stuck trauma might end up being re-traumatizing. So it's extremely important that the safety state is developed enough to handle whatever you have inside of you. It can be potentially disastrous to delve into your stuck trauma, into the inner pain, without being prepared for it, and part of that preparation is having a stronger vagal brake.

When you delve inward and do some unstucking, emotions come up. Memories come up. Sensations and impulses attached to the things you've been through come up. So we want the safety state active, to be able to actually experience whatever is coming up and tolerate it.

If you can't, that causes dysregulation and really just reinforces your stuck state, at least for the time being. There's even a good chance that when these things come up, you'll turn or return to maladaptive coping mechanisms, which in polyvagal language we call behavioral adaptations. Turning to behavioral adaptations stifles the defensive state from continuing to surface and discharge, and from self-regulation happening. Those behavioral adaptations keep you stuck in the defensive state.
But with the safety state active and strong enough, you can more mindfully experience the underlying impulse that's driving those behavioral adaptations.

blocks.h: Benefit two: more distress tolerance for the basics of life

blocks.p: The second benefit is greater distress tolerance for the basics in life. Not working on stuck trauma, just getting through the day-to-day stuff.

Irritations will be less irritating. Things that are triggering for you will be less triggering. The person who cuts you off on the road is less triggering. Someone in your home is snappy with you, talking to you in a harsh tone, maybe because they're having a bad day. From your safety state, you'll be able to roll with that a bit better, and maybe even be empathetic or compassionate. It won't be a personal thing. It'll be less triggering, less irritating, less upsetting.

You'll have greater capacity to connect with others in your day-to-day experience, from your state of safety and social engagement. You'll be more empathetic. You'll be more attuned to other people's polyvagal state, and also to what they're feeling in that moment. And you'll be able to provide co-regulation to other people. Those passive biological cues of safety will emanate from you, and hopefully somebody else will pick up on them.

You'll also have more capacity day to day to connect with yourself. You'll have more understanding of your own feelings, maybe even more self-compassion. You'll be able to direct that connectedness, that impulse to connect, toward yourself and look inward in stillness. You might even be able to look at whatever defensive states are surfacing for you day to day, and be curious about them, interested, mindful, and actually notice, allow, and experience them.

Day to day, you'll have more well-roundedness, more flexibility. All of these pieces look like someone who has more patience, more ability to connect, someone who can actually relax, but also feel motivated. They have a greater range of what they're able to feel and experience. They can be relaxed in stillness, but they can also be energized, and maybe even a little aggressive in a play state. This person isn't a nonstop happiness and co-regulation machine. They're able to access their mixed states as well, and they're able to drop down the ladder and then self-regulate back up, day to day, with greater ease.

blocks.h: Benefit three: more distress tolerance for new challenges

blocks.p: The third benefit is greater distress tolerance for new challenges in life. Not working on trauma, not the day-to-day stuff, but the big new challenges and milestones in life. You'll be better prepared to handle them.

When you develop your vagal brake, you're more prepared for new challenges. Not only that, you'll have more motivation to seek out new challenges, and more motivation and capacity for growth. And as you seek out those opportunities for challenge and growth, you're going to identify along the way what you need to work on.

Maybe you want to go back to school. Maybe you need to end a toxic relationship, and you've been putting it off. Maybe you need to set firmer boundaries with somebody. Maybe you want to start a new YouTube channel. These are all new challenges, and they can trigger that defensive state. Things that are new, different, and challenging will trigger that defensive state.

These challenges will present obstacles to your nervous system. They'll probably take you a bit out of your safety state. Some of that is very practical, like deciding what type of camera or microphone to get for your new YouTube channel. But they can also bring a more emotionally challenging challenge, like facing the fear of telling your parents you need more space, or saying no at work to someone who needs to hear it. These situations will challenge your distress tolerance. The greater the distress tolerance you have from a strong enough safety state, the more capacity you'll have to meet these challenges successfully.

I hope we're all identifying new growth points: challenges, milestones, or obstacles in life that challenge our capacity to self-regulate through them. And as we succeed, we get more capacity to self-regulate. We build the strength of our safety state by going down the ladder a bit, into some dysregulation or challenge, and then self-regulating, succeeding, and coming back up the ladder. Maybe we even use our defensive state activation to meet these challenges.

This is something I'm working on for myself. I'm building my little business here: my courses, the content I create. I'm constantly confronted with new challenges, and some of them have brought up deeply ingrained issues around money that came from my family. Another challenge I have is a fear of success. There's also a fear of rejection from the people I want to serve, which is you. To meet the bigger goal of feeling successful in building my business, I have to deal with those themes from my life, the issues that trigger a defensive state within me.

As I develop my vagal brake strength, my ability to sit with the distress of these things increases. From where I was about a year ago to where I am now, my capacity to do that is a lot higher, and these things don't feel nearly as challenging to me now as they did then.
